## What you will do

A **silicon audience** is a panel of digital twins: a language model, given one
voter's record, predicts how that voter would answer a question about a
political message. The Talking to Machines group uses such panels to decide
which message reaches which voter *before* the message runs, and it is testing
the panels against the people they are built from in a pre-registered study
(OSF, 7 October 2026).

In this notebook a language model writes a thirty-second television ad, and you
improve the instructions it is given, in three stages. Every ad is aimed at one
of five kinds of Ohio voter, from strong Democrats to strong Republicans, and
every ad gets two scores:

- **Does it read like a real ad?** Judges compare it with a real Ohio campaign
  ad and try to spot the machine-written one.
- **Does it hit its group?** The twins say how likely they would be to vote for
  the candidate behind it, and the ad should do better with its own group than
  with the other four.

The sections, in about forty-five minutes:

1. **The Voters:** the 400 Ohio twins you built this morning, in five groups;
2. **The question:** your issue, and the one question every twin answers;
3. **The study's scripts:** how the five groups rated the scripts in the
   pre-registered study, and how to read a score that is about *aim*;
4. **Stage 1:** a basic prompt writes five ads, one per group;
5. **Stage 2:** the same prompt with what our tests taught us added;
6. **Stage 3:** your prompt, run live: push the aim higher than Stage 2;
7. **The leaderboard,** and what the loop does next;
8. **What a twin cannot know.**

Stages 1 and 2, and one worked example of Stage 3, were run once by the
organisers and ship with the notebook, so
the same prompt gives everyone the same ads and the same scores. Only Stage 3
calls a language model, and only if an API key is set. Everything else runs
offline from the files beside this notebook.

**How to read this notebook.** As in the morning's notebooks, every table, text
block and figure the code prints has a number, given in bold just above the code
that prints it, and the text says which table, row or column a number comes
from.

**Figure 0.1.** The loop. The optimiser runs the ring over hundreds of
messages; this notebook walks it by hand, three times, with the audience and the
question already built.

```{r libs}
library(data.table)
library(jsonlite)
library(ggplot2)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
OUT  <- file.path("..", "output")
dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE)

read_parquet <- function(f) {           # arrow on the workshop server; nanoparquet is a light fallback
  if (requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE)) as.data.table(arrow::read_parquet(f))
  else as.data.table(nanoparquet::read_parquet(f))
}
GROUPS <- data.table(
  group  = c("SD", "WD", "IND", "WR", "SR"),
  label  = c("Strong Democrat", "Weak or leaning Democrat", "Independent",
             "Weak or leaning Republican", "Strong Republican"),
  phrase = c("strong Democrats", "weak or leaning Democrats", "independents",
             "weak or leaning Republicans", "strong Republicans"))
GROUP_COLOURS <- c(SD = "#1f4e9c", WD = "#7fa6dd", IND = "#8c8c8c", WR = "#e39a8f", SR = "#b0281a")
```

## 1. The Voters

The audience is the 400-twin Ohio panel from Workshop 1: a seeded draw from the
census frame, each twin matched to a Cooperative Election Study respondent and
rendered as a persona. The panel ships with this notebook as a copy, so you do
not need the morning's `output/` folder, but it is the same 400 twins with the
same personas, character for character.

Every persona carries the matched respondent's own **party identification** on
the seven-point scale. The block below reads it from the persona and puts each
twin in one of five groups: strong Democrats; weak or leaning Democrats;
independents; weak or leaning Republicans; strong Republicans. A twin whose
respondent answered "not sure" is in none of the five and is left out of the
group tables.

**Table 1.1.** `panel`: the 400 twins, by party identification and the group it
puts them in.

```{r panel}
panel <- read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "oh_panel_400.parquet"))
panel[, pid7 := sub("^- Party identification: ", "",
                    regmatches(persona_text, regexpr("- Party identification: [^\n]+", persona_text)))]
PID_TO_GROUP <- c("Strong Democrat" = "SD", "Not Very Strong Democrat" = "WD", "Lean Democrat" = "WD",
                  "Independent" = "IND",
                  "Lean Republican" = "WR", "Not Very Strong Republican" = "WR", "Strong Republican" = "SR")
panel[, group := unname(PID_TO_GROUP[pid7])]
panel[, .N, by = .(pid7, group)][order(match(group, GROUPS$group))]
```

The next block prints one persona in full: this is everything the twin is told
about who it is, exactly as the morning's model read it. Change `TWIN` to read
another. Notice the provenance line at the head of each section — modelled from
the census cell, or the matched respondent's own answer — and notice what is
*not* there: no advertisement, no rating of one, nothing about this study.

**Text 1.1.** The persona of twin `TWIN`.

```{r persona, comment = ""}
TWIN <- panel$twin_id[1]
cat(panel[twin_id == TWIN, persona_text])
```

## 2. The question

Pick one of the two issues in Table 2.1 and put it in `ISSUE`. Every ad you see
from here on is about that issue.

**Table 2.1.** `issues`: the two issues in this block.

```{r issue}
issues <- fread(file.path(DATA, "issues.csv"))[key %in% c("COST", "IMM")]
ISSUE  <- "immigration"     # or "taxes and household relief"
it <- issues[issue == ISSUE]
issues[, .(key, issue, title)]
```

Every ad is put to every twin with **one question**: how likely this person
would be to vote for the candidate behind the ad, from 0 (certainly not) to 10
(certainly would). It is the vote-likelihood item of the pre-registered study,
word for word.

The **header** tells the model what it is doing: *predicting* the answer a
particular person would give, in the third person ("this person"), from that
person's record. That is how the registered study puts it, and it is not the
same as asking the model to *be* the person. The **profile** is the persona you
read in Text 1.1; then comes the ad, and the question. The twin is never told
which group an ad was written for, who wrote it, or what the study is about.

The block below defines the header, the question and the JSON schema the answer
must match, and prints them.

**Text 2.1.** The question, as sent (the profile omitted).

```{r question, comment = ""}
HEADER <- paste(
  "Below is the profile of an adult in Ohio, and then a political advertisement. Predict how this",
  "person would answer the question that follows: give the answer this person would actually give,",
  "not the answer a typical person would give, and not the one you would wish them to give.",
  "Return only the JSON object described at the end.")

question_block <- function(script) paste0(
  "Here is the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office.\n\n",
  script, "\n\n",
  "After reading this, how likely would this person be to vote for the candidate behind this advertisement?\n",
  "0 = certainly not, 10 = certainly would.\n",
  "Return: {\"ptv\": <0-10>}")

SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = list("ptv"),
               properties = list(ptv = list(type = "integer", minimum = 0, maximum = 10)))

cat(HEADER, "\n\n=== PROFILE ===\n{persona_text}\n=== END OF PROFILE ===\n\n", sep = "")
cat(question_block("{script}"))
```

## 3. The study's scripts, by group

Before writing anything, look at what the group's own message factory wrote.
The pre-registered study fields fifteen scripts: for each of three issues, four
written for positions 20, 40, 60 and 80 on a left–right scale for that issue,
and one **untargeted** script on a different matter altogether, the control.
They were frozen with the registration, and all fifteen have already been put to
all 400 twins.

One caution about these answers. They were generated before the registration was
finalised, with an earlier interview that asked the model to answer *as* the
person, and with four questions rather than one. Only the vote-likelihood answer
is used here.

The block below defines the scoring used in the rest of the notebook, and prints
nothing:

- `group_means()` gives each ad's mean vote likelihood (0–10) in each of the
  five groups;
- `aim()` gives each ad's **aim**: the mean in the group it was written for,
  minus the average of the means in the other four groups.

```{r scoring}
read_jsonl <- function(f) {
  if (!file.exists(f) || length(readLines(f, warn = FALSE)) == 0) return(data.table())
  rbindlist(lapply(readLines(f, warn = FALSE), function(l) as.data.table(fromJSON(l))), fill = TRUE)
}
group_means <- function(ans) {
  d <- merge(ans, panel[!is.na(group), .(twin_id, group)], by = "twin_id")
  d[, .(n = .N, ptv = round(mean(ptv), 2)), by = .(ad_id, group)]
}
aim <- function(gm, targets) {               # targets: ad_id, target (a group)
  d <- merge(gm, targets[, .(ad_id, target)], by = "ad_id")
  d[, .(target_ptv = ptv[group == target[1]],
        others_ptv = round(mean(ptv[group != target[1]]), 2)), by = .(ad_id, target)][
    , aim := round(target_ptv - others_ptv, 2)][]
}
```

The next block reads the cached answers and prints the five group means for the
five scripts on your issue, one row per script.

**Table 3.1.** `study`: mean vote likelihood by group, for the study's scripts on
your issue.

```{r study-scripts}
study_ads <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ads_frozen.csv"))[issue == ISSUE]
study_ads[, script := ifelse(arm == "targeted", paste("position", target_position), "untargeted")]
cached <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "ad_answers.jsonl"))[ad_id %in% study_ads$ad_id, .(twin_id, ad_id, ptv = as.numeric(ptv))]
study <- merge(group_means(cached), study_ads[, .(ad_id, script)], by = "ad_id")
dcast(study, ad_id + script ~ factor(group, levels = GROUPS$group), value.var = "ptv")
```

**Figure 3.1.** The same, as five bars per script: one bar per group, strong
Democrats on the left, strong Republicans on the right.

```{r study-plot}
ggplot(study, aes(x = factor(group, levels = GROUPS$group), y = ptv, fill = group)) +
  geom_col() + facet_wrap(~ script, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(NULL) + scale_y_continuous("Mean vote likelihood, 0-10", limits = c(0, 10)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 3.1.** Suppose you had to pick one of these five scripts to win over
**weak or leaning Republicans** (`WR`). Which script has the highest mean with
that group in Table 3.1? Now compute each script's **aim** for that group with
`aim(study, study_ads[, .(ad_id, target = "WR")])`. Is the script with the
highest bar also the script with the best aim? Why might they differ?

---

## 4. Stage 1: the basic prompt

From here on a language model writes the ads. The factory is a single call to
the workshop model with a prompt printed in full below: one prompt, one call,
no hidden machinery. `{issue}` and `{group}` are filled in for each ad, so one
prompt writes five ads, one per group.

The block below reads your key and the proxy address from the environment,
defines the prompts and the model calls, and prints the Stage 1 prompt.

- `fill()` puts the issue and the group into a prompt;
- `write_ads()` sends a filled prompt for each group and returns the five ads.
  The workshop model sometimes declines to write a political ad aimed at a
  named group of voters ("Sorry, I can't create targeted political
  persuasion…"); when it does, `write_ads()` asks again, up to three times, and
  column `asked` records how many tries each ad took. An ad still declined after
  three tries is marked `declined` and is not scored;
- `run_ads()` puts each ad to the audience and to the judges (below).

**Text 4.1.** The Stage 1 prompt.

```{r prompts, comment = ""}
MODEL <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"
key   <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")
base  <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL", unset = "https://api.openai.com/v1")
API   <- paste0(sub("/+$", "", base), "/chat/completions")

STAGE1 <- paste(
  "Write the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office in Ohio.",
  "75 to 85 words, spoken by the candidate in the first person, ending with \"And I approve this message.\"",
  "Name no candidate, party or office. The advertisement is about {issue}. It should win the vote of {group} in Ohio.")
STAGE2_ADD <- paste(
  "Write it the way a real candidate speaks. Say once, flatly, what you did before politics that gives you the right",
  "to talk about this: a job, a service, a business. Put in one concrete scene or detail, a person, a street, a price,",
  "invented but with nobody named. Promise what you will do in plain verbs, naming the instrument, never \"fix\" or",
  "\"stand up to\". Short spoken sentences, contractions, no hedging, no balancing the other side, no neat parallel",
  "closing line.")
EXAMPLE_ADD <- "Mention one thing the voter can check for themselves."    # the worked example of Stage 3 (Section 6)

fill <- function(prompt, group) paste0(
  gsub("{group}", GROUPS$phrase[match(group, GROUPS$group)], gsub("{issue}", it$issue, prompt, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE),
  "\n\nReturn the script only.")

chat <- function(messages, response_format = NULL) {
  body <- list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low", messages = messages)
  if (!is.null(response_format)) body$response_format <- response_format
  httr2::request(API) |> httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(key) |> httr2::req_body_json(body) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> httr2::req_timeout(120)
}
perform_all <- function(reqs, workers = 8) {
  if (packageVersion("httr2") >= "1.1.0") httr2::req_perform_parallel(reqs, on_error = "continue", max_active = workers, progress = FALSE)
  else httr2::req_perform_parallel(reqs, pool = curl::new_pool(total_con = workers, host_con = workers), on_error = "continue", progress = FALSE)
}
content_of <- function(r) if (inherits(r, "error") || is.null(r)) NA_character_ else
  trimws(httr2::resp_body_json(r)$choices[[1]]$message$content)
n_words <- function(x) lengths(strsplit(x, "\\s+"))

is_ad <- function(x) !is.na(x) & grepl("approve this message", x, ignore.case = TRUE) &
  !grepl("^\\W*(sorry|i'm sorry|i am sorry|i can.?t|i cannot)", x, ignore.case = TRUE)

write_ads <- function(prompt, id_prefix, tries = 3) {    # asks again, up to `tries` times, for any ad the model declined
  text <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(GROUPS)); asked <- integer(nrow(GROUPS))
  for (t in seq_len(tries)) {
    todo <- which(!is_ad(text))
    if (!length(todo)) break
    reqs <- lapply(GROUPS$group[todo], function(g) chat(list(list(role = "user", content = fill(prompt, g)))))
    text[todo] <- vapply(perform_all(reqs), content_of, character(1)); asked[todo] <- t
  }
  data.table(ad_id = paste0(id_prefix, "_", GROUPS$group), issue = it$key, target = GROUPS$group,
             prompt = prompt, text = text, asked = asked, declined = !is_ad(text))[, words := n_words(text)][]
}

cat(strwrap(STAGE1, width = 90), sep = "\n")
```

### The audience and the judges

Four hundred twins is more than a live round needs. The next block draws the
**audience** for every ad in Stages 1 to 3: ten twins from each group, fifty in
all, with a fixed seed so that everyone in the room scores on the same fifty.

It also loads the **real ads**: ten thirty-second campaign spots, nine from Ohio
and one from Illinois, taken from Google's political-ad archive with the
candidates' names removed (five Republican, five Democratic). They are what the
judges compare each machine-written ad with. Each ad is shown to **forty
judges**, separate calls to the same model, each with one real ad, and each
judge is asked which of the two is the real one. Every machine-written ad meets
each of the ten real ads four times: twice with the real ad shown first (text A)
and twice with it shown second (text B). The order matters because the judges lean
towards text A, and showing each pairing both ways means that lean weighs the
same on every ad. An ad's
**spotted** score is the share of its judges who picked the real ad correctly:
0.5 is what guessing gives, so an ad near 0.5 or below reads like a real one,
and 1 means every judge saw through it. An ad **passes** if at least one judge
was fooled.

The block prints the judge's instruction, and one real ad so you can hear what
the judges hear.

**Text 4.2.** The judge's instruction, and one of the real ads.

```{r audience, comment = ""}
set.seed(2026)
audience <- panel[!is.na(group), .SD[sample(.N, 10)], by = group]
real_ads <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "real_ads_judges.jsonl"))
N_JUDGES <- 40

JUDGE <- paste(
  "You are shown two texts. Each is the spoken words of a thirty-second American political advertisement.",
  "One of them is a real advertisement that a candidate's campaign put on the air. The other was written",
  "by a machine imitating one. Names have been removed from both.\nSay which one is the real advertisement.\n",
  "Return only: {\"real\": \"A\" or \"B\", \"confidence\": <50-100>}")
JUDGE_SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = c("real", "confidence"),
                     properties = list(real = list(type = "string", enum = list("A", "B")),
                                       confidence = list(type = "integer", minimum = 50, maximum = 100)))

twin_request <- function(persona_text, script) chat(
  list(list(role = "system", content = HEADER),
       list(role = "user", content = paste0("=== PROFILE ===\n", persona_text, "\n=== END OF PROFILE ===\n\n", question_block(script)))),
  response_format = list(type = "json_schema", json_schema = list(name = "ptv", strict = TRUE, schema = SCHEMA)))
judge_pairs <- function(id) {                # every real ad in both slots, A and B; the same draw for the same ad, every run
  set.seed(sum(utf8ToInt(id) * seq_along(utf8ToInt(id))))
  grid <- CJ(ref_id = real_ads$ref_id, real_pos = c("A", "B"))
  grid <- grid[rep(seq_len(.N), ceiling(N_JUDGES / .N))][sample(.N)][seq_len(N_JUDGES)]
  data.table(ad_id = id, judge = seq_len(N_JUDGES), grid)
}
judge_request <- function(machine, real, real_pos) chat(
  list(list(role = "user", content = paste0(JUDGE, "\n\nText A:\n", if (real_pos == "A") real else machine,
                                            "\n\nText B:\n", if (real_pos == "A") machine else real))),
  response_format = list(type = "json_schema", json_schema = list(name = "judge", strict = TRUE, schema = JUDGE_SCHEMA)))

run_ads <- function(ads) {                   # ads: ad_id, text. 50 twins + 40 judges per ad, all in parallel
  tw <- CJ(ad = seq_len(nrow(ads)), k = seq_len(nrow(audience)))
  jp <- rbindlist(lapply(ads$ad_id, judge_pairs))
  reqs <- c(lapply(seq_len(nrow(tw)), function(r) twin_request(audience$persona_text[tw$k[r]], ads$text[tw$ad[r]])),
            lapply(seq_len(nrow(jp)), function(r) judge_request(ads[ad_id == jp$ad_id[r], text],
                                                                real_ads[ref_id == jp$ref_id[r], text], jp$real_pos[r])))
  resps <- perform_all(reqs)
  failed <- vapply(resps, function(r) inherits(r, "error") || is.null(r), logical(1))
  first_error <- if (any(failed)) conditionMessage(resps[[which(failed)[1]]]) else NA_character_
  out <- vapply(resps, content_of, character(1))
  t_out <- out[seq_len(nrow(tw))]; j_out <- out[nrow(tw) + seq_len(nrow(jp))]
  answers <- tw[, .(ad_id = ads$ad_id[ad], twin_id = audience$twin_id[k], persona_sha256 = audience$persona_sha256[k],
                    ptv = vapply(t_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(fromJSON(x)$ptv), numeric(1)),
                    model = MODEL)][!is.na(ptv)]
  jp[, `:=`(pick = vapply(j_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_character_ else fromJSON(x)$real, character(1)),
            confidence = vapply(j_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(fromJSON(x)$confidence), numeric(1)),
            model = MODEL)]
  jp[, spotted := pick == real_pos]
  list(answers = answers, judges = jp[!is.na(pick)], failed = sum(failed), first_error = first_error)
}
scoreboard <- function(ads, answers, judges) {
  a <- aim(group_means(answers), ads)
  s <- judges[, .(judges = .N, spotted = round(mean(spotted), 2)), by = ad_id]
  d <- merge(merge(ads[, .(ad_id, target)], a[, .(ad_id, target_ptv, others_ptv, aim)], by = "ad_id"), s, by = "ad_id")
  d[, passes := spotted < 1][order(match(target, GROUPS$group))]
}
five_bars <- function(ads, answers) {
  gm <- merge(group_means(answers), ads[, .(ad_id, target)], by = "ad_id")
  gm[, panel := paste("written for", GROUPS$label[match(target, GROUPS$group)])]
  gm[, panel := factor(panel, levels = paste("written for", GROUPS$label))]
  ggplot(gm, aes(x = factor(group, levels = GROUPS$group), y = ptv, fill = group, alpha = group == target)) +
    geom_col() + facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
    scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
    scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.35), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_discrete(NULL) + scale_y_continuous("Mean vote likelihood, 0-10", limits = c(0, 10)) +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))
}
spotted_adjusted <- function(sbs, judges) {  # each ad and each prompt pooled, with real ad x slot fixed effects
  key <- rbindlist(lapply(names(sbs), function(n) sbs[[n]][, .(ad_id, prompt = n, target)]))
  j <- merge(judges[, .(ad_id, ref_id, real_pos, spotted = as.numeric(spotted))], key, by = "ad_id")
  j[, cell := interaction(ref_id, real_pos)]
  est <- function(unit) {                    # unit means at the average real ad and slot, and their 95% intervals
    s <- coef(summary(lm(as.formula(paste("spotted ~ 0 +", unit, "+ cell")), data = j, contrasts = list(cell = "contr.sum"))))
    s <- s[startsWith(rownames(s), unit), , drop = FALSE]
    data.table(id = sub(paste0("^", unit), "", rownames(s)), spotted = s[, 1], lo = s[, 1] - 1.96 * s[, 2], hi = s[, 1] + 1.96 * s[, 2])
  }
  rbind(merge(key, est("ad_id"), by.x = "ad_id", by.y = "id")[, .(prompt, target, spotted, lo, hi)],
        est("prompt")[, .(prompt = id, target = "ALL", spotted, lo, hi)])
}
spotted_bars <- function(sbs, judges) {      # sbs: named list of scoreboards, one per prompt, drawn left to right
  d <- spotted_adjusted(sbs, judges)
  d[, prompt := factor(prompt, levels = names(sbs))]
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(d, aes(x = factor(target, levels = c(GROUPS$group, "ALL")), y = spotted, fill = target, alpha = prompt, group = prompt)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = dodge, width = 0.25, alpha = 1, colour = "grey20") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 5.5, colour = "grey70") +
    scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c(GROUP_COLOURS, ALL = "#333333"), guide = "none") +
    scale_alpha_manual(NULL, values = seq(0.35, 1, length.out = length(sbs))) +
    scale_x_discrete("Ad written for", labels = c(GROUPS$group, "All five\npooled")) +
    scale_y_continuous("Spotted: share of judges who picked the real ad", breaks = seq(0.25, 1, 0.25)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.25, 1)) +
    theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")
}

cat(JUDGE, "\n\n")
cat(real_ads$ref_id[1], " (", real_ads$party[1], ", ", real_ads$state[1], ", ", real_ads$words[1], " words)\n\n", sep = "")
cat(strwrap(real_ads$text[1], width = 90), sep = "\n")
```

### What Stage 1 wrote

The next block reads the Stage 1 ads for your issue from the stored run and
prints them, one per group.

**Text 4.3.** The five Stage 1 ads.

```{r stage1-ads, comment = ""}
STAGE_ADS     <- fread(file.path(DATA, "stage_ads.csv"))
STAGE_ANSWERS <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "stage_answers.jsonl"))
STAGE_JUDGES  <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "stage_judges.jsonl"))
show_ads <- function(ads) for (i in seq_len(nrow(ads))) {
  cat(sprintf("%s — written for %s (%d words)\n", ads$ad_id[i], GROUPS$phrase[match(ads$target[i], GROUPS$group)], ads$words[i]))
  cat(strwrap(ads$text[i], width = 90, prefix = "   "), sep = "\n"); cat("\n")
}
s1 <- STAGE_ADS[stage == 1 & issue == it$key]
show_ads(s1)
```

**Figure 4.1.** How the five groups rated each Stage 1 ad. Each panel is one ad;
the bar of the group it was written for is solid, the other four are pale. A
well-aimed ad has its solid bar standing above the pale ones; an ad whose solid
bar is merely high, with the pale bars just as high, pleases everyone and aims
at no one.

```{r stage1-plot}
five_bars(s1, STAGE_ANSWERS)
```

**Table 4.1.** Stage 1 scores: `aim` (the target group's mean, `target_ptv`,
minus the average of the other four, `others_ptv`), `spotted` (the share of the
forty judges who picked the real ad) and `passes` (at least one judge fooled).

```{r stage1-score}
sb1 <- scoreboard(s1, STAGE_ANSWERS, STAGE_JUDGES)
sb1
```

## 5. Stage 2: what our tests taught us

The group ran these ads past judges many times before the workshop. Stage 2 is
the Stage 1 prompt with one paragraph added, printed below with the one sentence
that explains it.

**Text 5.1.** What Stage 2 adds to the Stage 1 prompt.

```{r stage2-prompt, comment = ""}
cat(strwrap(STAGE2_ADD, width = 90), sep = "\n")
cat("\nIn our tests, this is what set real candidates' ads apart from machine-written ones.\n")
```

**Text 5.2.** The five Stage 2 ads, from the stored run.

```{r stage2-ads, comment = ""}
s2 <- STAGE_ADS[stage == 2 & issue == it$key]
show_ads(s2)
```

**Figure 5.1.** How the five groups rated each Stage 2 ad, drawn as in Figure
4.1.

```{r stage2-plot}
five_bars(s2, STAGE_ANSWERS)
```

**Table 5.1.** Stage 1 against Stage 2, ad by ad: the aim and the spotted score
of each stage side by side.

```{r stage2-score}
sb2 <- scoreboard(s2, STAGE_ANSWERS, STAGE_JUDGES)
merge(sb1[, .(target, aim_stage1 = aim, spotted_stage1 = spotted)],
      sb2[, .(target, aim_stage2 = aim, spotted_stage2 = spotted)], by = "target")[order(match(target, GROUPS$group))]
```

**Figure 5.2.** The spotted columns of Table 5.1 as bars: for each group, the
Stage 1 ad (pale) and the Stage 2 ad (solid), and on the right the five ads of
each stage pooled. A lower bar is harder to spot; the dashed line at 0.5 is
what guessing gives. The black lines are 95% confidence intervals.

```{r stage2-spotted-plot}
spotted_bars(list(`Stage 1` = sb1, `Stage 2` = sb2), STAGE_JUDGES)
```

*Note to Figure 5.2.* Each bar is a share of judge calls: of the 40 calls for
one ad, or the 200 for the five pooled, the share in which the judge picked the
real ad. Much of the noise in that share has a known source. Which real ad a
judge saw, and whether it was shown first or second, moves the chance of a
correct pick more than anything else: some real ads are picked almost every
time when shown first and almost never when shown second. Every machine-written
ad meets the same real ads in the same slots, so this does not favour any ad,
and the intervals take it out. They come from a linear regression of each
call's `spotted` (1 if the judge picked the real ad, 0 if not) on one indicator
for each ad, or for each stage in the pooled bars, and one fixed effect for
each pairing of real ad and slot (A or B), coded to sum to zero; because every
ad meets each pairing equally often, each ad's coefficient is exactly its share.
The intervals are the coefficient plus and minus 1.96 standard errors, with the
residual variance pooled over all the calls in the figure, so every ad's
interval has the same width. They take the ads as given: they measure how much
a share would move with another set of judges for *these* ads, not the larger
variation that would come from the model writing a different ad from the same
prompt. Whether the Stage 2 prompt would also beat Stage 1 with five other ads
is a question only more ads can answer.

**Exercise 5.1.** Did the Stage 2 paragraph make the ads harder to spot, on
average across the five rows of Table 5.1 and in Figure 5.2? Did it cost
anything in aim? Read
one Stage 2 ad next to its Stage 1 version and name one thing the paragraph
changed.

## 6. Stage 3: sharpen the aim

Now it is yours. Stage 2 gave you five ads, each with an aim in Table 5.1. The
goal of Stage 3 is to push that aim higher: each ad should do even better with
its own group, and worse with the other four, than its Stage 2 version did.
Keep an eye on the judges while you do it. An ad the judges see through every
time does not pass, and only passing ads go on the room's leaderboard
(Section 7), however well they are aimed.

The prompt is plain text, and every word of it is yours to change: add a rule,
delete one, rewrite the voice, start again from nothing. Only `{issue}` and
`{group}` must stay, because they are where the issue and the group go.

### A worked example

Before you write your own, here is one Stage 3 run the organisers made ahead of
time: the Stage 2 prompt with one sentence added at the end, printed below. It
was run once, like Stages 1 and 2, and ships with the notebook, so everyone has
a Stage 3 run to read whether or not the live calls work. One sentence is the
smallest change there is; yours can be as large as you like.

**Text 6.1.** The worked example: the sentence it adds to the Stage 2 prompt,
and its five ads.

```{r example-ads, comment = ""}
cat("Stage 2 prompt, plus:", EXAMPLE_ADD, "\n\n")
sx <- STAGE_ADS[stage == 3 & issue == it$key]
show_ads(sx)
sbx <- scoreboard(sx, STAGE_ANSWERS, STAGE_JUDGES)
```

**Table 6.1.** Stage 2 against the worked example, ad by ad: the aim and the
spotted score of each side by side.

```{r example-score}
merge(sb2[, .(target, aim_stage2 = aim, spotted_stage2 = spotted)],
      sbx[, .(target, aim_example = aim, spotted_example = spotted)], by = "target")[order(match(target, GROUPS$group))]
```

Read Table 6.1 the way the goal asks: for which groups is `aim_example` above
`aim_stage2`, and did `spotted_example` stay below 1, so that the ad still
passes?

### Your turn

**Exercise 6.1.** `MY_PROMPT` below starts as the Stage 2 prompt. Change it so
that each ad lands harder with its own group, and run the block. Compare your
row in Table 6.2 with the Stage 2 row: is `mean_aim` higher, and is `passing`
no lower? Write that row down. Then move your run out of the way (below), change
one thing, run it again, and say which change moved which score. In Figure 6.1,
did the solid bars rise, or did the pale bars fall?

The block writes five new ads with your prompt, one per group, puts each to the
same fifty twins and to forty judges, and saves everything to `output/` in three
files: `stage3_ads.csv`, `stage3_answers.jsonl` and `stage3_judges.jsonl`. That is
5 ads, 250 twin answers and 200 judge calls, a minute or two. With no key the
block prints your prompt and stops; the worked example above still shows what a
Stage 3 run looks like.

Once those files exist, the block makes no new calls: running it again, or
knitting the notebook, shows the saved run, so your results stay the same each
time. To make a new run, with a new prompt or the same one again, first move the
three files into a folder of their own, for example `output/run1/` (in the
RStudio Files pane: tick them, then More > Move), and run the block again.

**Text 6.2.** Your prompt, and the five ads it wrote.

```{r stage3, comment = ""}
MY_PROMPT <- paste(STAGE1, STAGE2_ADD)     # edit me, then re-run this block

S3_ADS     <- file.path(OUT, "stage3_ads.csv")
S3_ANSWERS <- file.path(OUT, "stage3_answers.jsonl")
S3_JUDGES  <- file.path(OUT, "stage3_judges.jsonl")
short_hash <- function(x) { if (requireNamespace("digest", quietly = TRUE)) substr(digest::digest(x, algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE), 1, 6)
                            else sprintf("%06x", sum(utf8ToInt(x) * seq_along(utf8ToInt(x))) %% 16777216) }
append_jsonl <- function(d, f) for (i in seq_len(nrow(d))) cat(toJSON(as.list(d[i]), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA), "\n", file = f, append = TRUE, sep = "")
read_s3_ads <- function(f) {                 # fread can keep a CSV's doubled quotes ("") inside text; undo that
  if (!file.exists(f)) return(data.table())
  d <- fread(f)
  for (col in intersect(c("prompt", "text"), names(d))) set(d, j = col, value = gsub('""', '"', d[[col]], fixed = TRUE))
  d
}
saved_run <- any(file.exists(c(S3_ADS, S3_ANSWERS, S3_JUDGES)))

if (saved_run) {                             # a run is already saved: show it, never call the API again
  s3 <- read_s3_ads(S3_ADS)
  cat("A saved Stage 3 run is in output/, so this block shows it and makes no new calls.\n",
      "To make a new run, move stage3_ads.csv, stage3_answers.jsonl and stage3_judges.jsonl\n",
      "into a folder of their own (for example output/run1/) and run this block again.\n\n", sep = "")
  if (nrow(s3) && !identical(unique(s3$prompt), MY_PROMPT))
    cat("Note: MY_PROMPT has changed since the saved run. The ads below come from the saved run's prompt:\n\n",
        paste(strwrap(unique(s3$prompt)[1], width = 90), collapse = "\n"), "\n\n", sep = "")
  if (nrow(s3) && !any(s3$issue == it$key))
    cat("Note: the saved run is for the other issue, so Figure 6.1 and Table 6.2 have no Stage 3 run for this one.\n\n")
  show_ads(s3[issue == it$key])
} else {
cat(strwrap(MY_PROMPT, width = 90), sep = "\n"); cat("\n")
if (!all(grepl("{issue}", MY_PROMPT, fixed = TRUE), grepl("{group}", MY_PROMPT, fixed = TRUE))) {
  cat("Put {issue} and {group} back into MY_PROMPT: without them every ad is the same.\n")
} else if (nzchar(key)) {
  run_id <- paste0("S3_", it$key, "_", short_hash(MY_PROMPT))
  s3 <- write_ads(MY_PROMPT, run_id)
  if (any(s3$declined)) cat("The model declined to write the ad for:", paste(GROUPS$phrase[match(s3[declined == TRUE, target], GROUPS$group)], collapse = ", "),
                            "\n(three tries each). Those groups are left out of this run; soften the wording or run again.\n\n")
  s3 <- s3[declined == FALSE]
  s3[, stage := 3]
  res <- run_ads(s3)
  show_ads(s3)
  if (res$failed) cat(sprintf("%d of the %d twin and judge calls failed. The first error was:\n   %s\n\n",
                              res$failed, nrow(s3) * (nrow(audience) + N_JUDGES), res$first_error))
  if (nrow(res$answers) == 0 || nrow(res$judges) == 0) {
    cat("No twin answers or no judge calls came back, so this run cannot be scored and nothing was saved.",
        "Run the block again in a minute; if it fails again, ask a helper.\n")
  } else {
    fwrite(s3, S3_ADS)
    append_jsonl(res$answers, S3_ANSWERS); append_jsonl(res$judges, S3_JUDGES)
    cat(sprintf("%d ads, %d twin answers and %d judge calls saved to %s\n", nrow(s3), nrow(res$answers), nrow(res$judges), OUT))
  }
} else cat("No API key found; skipping Stage 3.\n")
}
```

**Figure 6.1.** How the five groups rated each of your ads, drawn as in Figure

```{r stage3-plot}
  s3_all <- data.table()
}
if (nrow(s3_all)) {
  last <- s3_all[ad_id %in% tail(s3_all$ad_id, 5)]
  print(five_bars(last, s3_ans))
} else cat("No Stage 3 run yet.\n")
```

**Table 6.2.** All three stages side by side, one row per prompt: Stages 1 and
2, the worked example, and the Stage 3 run saved in `output/`. Each row gives the
average aim of its five ads, the average spotted score, and how many of the five
pass. Your goal is a row whose `mean_aim` is above the Stage 2 row's, with
`passing` no lower.

```{r all-stages}
summ <- function(sb, label) sb[, .(stage = label, mean_aim = round(mean(aim), 2), mean_spotted = round(mean(spotted), 2), passing = sum(passes))]
rows <- list(summ(sb1, "1: basic"), summ(sb2, "2: our addition"), summ(sbx, "3: worked example"))
if (nrow(s3_all)) {
  s3_all[, run := sub("_[A-Z]+$", "", ad_id)]
  for (r in unique(s3_all$run)) rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- summ(scoreboard(s3_all[run == r], s3_ans, s3_jud), paste("3: yours,", r))
}
rbindlist(rows)
```

## 7. The leaderboard, and what the loop does next

The room's leaderboard is every Stage 3 ad written today that **passes** (at
least one judge was fooled), ranked by **aim**. The block below writes your
passing ads to a file the session collects at the end, so the leaderboard can go
on the screen.

**Table 7.1.** Your entries for the room's leaderboard.

```{r deposit}
if (nrow(s3_all)) {
  entry <- merge(scoreboard(s3_all, s3_ans, s3_jud)[passes == TRUE], s3_all[, .(ad_id, issue, text)], by = "ad_id")
  setorder(entry, -aim)
  entry[, user := Sys.getenv("USER", unset = "unknown")]
  fwrite(entry, file.path(OUT, paste0("leaderboard_", entry$user[1], ".csv")))
  entry[, .(ad_id, target, aim, spotted)]
} else cat("Nothing to deposit yet.")
```

What you ran three times by hand, the optimiser runs as a **search**: a
population of prompts and ads, scored on the full audience, the best kept, the
rest rewritten from what the audience and the judges said, for as many
generations as the budget allows, with the audience re-drawn so that the search
does not learn the quirks of fifty twins. The session now shows that loop
running. Two parts of it are not in this package and are not on GitHub: the
search itself — how prompts and ads are mutated and selected — and the tuning of
the audience sample. The construction of the twins, the question and the scoring
are all here, in the open, exactly as the group runs them. That line is drawn on
purpose, and it is drawn here so that you do not have to find it.

---

## 8. What a twin cannot know

Three things to carry out of the room.

The twin answers from a persona built from a census cell and a matched survey
respondent's own answers. It has never seen an advertisement rated by that
respondent, and it was told nothing about this study. When an ad scores well,
you can read the persona and see why; when it scores badly, the same.

Whether the twins' ratings match those of the people they are built from is an
open question, and the group is answering it the only way that counts: a
pre-registered study (OSF, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/CKAM2, 7 October 2026) in which
each human respondent rates the fifteen scripts of Section 3 on four questions,
and the model predicts that person's answers from their profile. Today you asked
one of those questions, vote likelihood, about ads a model wrote to your
instructions. Until the humans have answered, a leaderboard is a leaderboard of
twins. The judges are a model too: a judge may recognise a real ad from memory,
which works against you, and a human viewer may spot habits the judges miss.

And a choice worth noticing: this morning's vote module asked the model to
estimate *probabilities* about a record, as an analyst; this afternoon the model
predicted the *answer* a particular person would give, on the scale that person
sees. They are different instruments, and a method that cannot say which it used
is not a method. The registered study uses the second.
